Its trunks and branches brew a sense of the traditional Japanese aesthetics of ”wabi” and ”sabi.” So, whether ”mochikomi” is old or not will decide the value of the tree.

Degrading. It refers to a tree that grows too much, peaks out as bonsai, and becomes unable to maintain its tree shape. ”Mochikuzusu” also means that a bonsai tree’s shape will deteriorate after branches or other key elements are broken.

Pinching out buds. It refers to the work of pinching out new buds in early spring to curb excessive growth of tree tops or branches and make a tree grow evenly. There are two methods to pinch out new buds. One is to cut out new buds with scissors after the buds come out to a certain extent. The other is to cut strong buds open with tweezers and take them away shortly before they start to sprout. In both methods, the key is to trim buds before they become firm and while they are still soft. If the buds are forcibly taken away after they become firm, the buds will be lost or the bud root will turn red and look ugly. So attention should be paid to avoid such an outcome.

”Metsugi” is a grafting technique and refers to grafting of buds of a tree into branches and trunks. After cutting into a ”daiki” stock tree or cutting its bark open, a ”tsugiho” scion made up of buds of ”hogi” plant tissue in wedge shape will be inserted and fixed there. A number of buds can be grafted onto a single tree. As results can be obtained in a short period of time, re-grafting can be done in the same term. Non-coalescent buds turn darkish 10 to 15 days after the ”metsugi” grafting process. ”Metsugi” work is best carried out from August to September.

Bud trimming. It refers to the work of trimming new buds to balance the strength of bud growth in pine trees, such as ”kuromatsu” (Japanese Black Pine). ”Mekiri” bud-trimming work is not uniform and varies depending on the species of tree and timing of the season. A single round of ”mekiri” work is necessary once a year for a tree that grows slowly. But the process needs to be done frequently for trees exhibiting fast growth.

”Meosae” refers to the work of curving downward new buds with wires that come out in early spring. This work is important to shape tree form, especially for young trees which vigorously send out fresh buds. In most species of tree, new buds that come out in the early spring extend upward obliquely. If the situation is left untouched, growers cannot shape bonsai trees as they might like.

”Meokoshi” is a technical term for ”hariganekake” wiring work. It refers to the work of picking a bud at the tip of a branch with wires and shaping a tree, mainly of ”shohaku” evergreen pines. This work is aimed at expressing a sense of dynamism and improving the appearance of a tree. It is also effective in improving ventilation and catching more sunlight. Sunlight to the root of a bud greatly improves the sprouting of a new bud.

”Meatari” refers to small buds that sprout from places that would not usually send out buds, following ”mekiri” or ”metsumi” bud-trimming work. These buds will grow into branches, but such buds should be cut, except for those whose branches are necessary.

Chamber. It refers to facilities to protect bonsai trees against damage from frost, freezing or snow in the winter season. A prefabricated house, plastic greenhouse or any other closed chamber is fine for such ”muro” facilities. But attention must be paid to maintain proper indoor temperatures in such facilities. The suitable indoor temperature is said to be around 15 C (or 59 F). The indoor temperature should be adjusted through ventilation. It is important to put a bonsai tree into a ”muro” chamber as late as possible and take it out as early as possible. A bonsai tree should be managed in a natural environment as much as possible. Excessive protection should be avoided.

Literally, green picking. It refers to the work of trimming of fresh buds that have yet to send out leaves. In general, the work is done in early spring for ”kuromatsu” (Japanese Black Pine), ”akamatsu” (Japanese Red Pine) and ”goyomatsu” (Japanese White Pine) trees. These pine trees sprout one or more new buds, called ”midori,” from the top of a branch yearly. The number of ”midori” buds differs, depending on the tree’s stems. If the buds are left untouched, branches will extend too long and ”kurumaeda” wheel-like branches appear on the tree. (”Kurumaeda refers to branches sprouting from a certain point like spokes of a wheel. It is among ”imieda” unwanted branches in bonsai cultivation.) So growers need to cut unnecessary buds and adjust the number and growth of branches to produce a proper balance for a bonsai tree.

Living portion. It refers to living portions of a trunk on ”shimpaku” (Sargent’s Juniper) and ”tosho” (Japanese Needle Juniper) trees which have ”jin” bleached trunks or ”shari” withered branches or tree tops. The ”jin” and ”shari” portions that have died will not draw water. ”Mizusui” refers to living portions of a truck that will draw water.

Watering, the most important process to grow a bonsai tree. Water supply is essential for a bonsai tree that is grown in a limited space of a pot. Many people say it takes three years to attain the watering technique. There is no perfect manual for watering. Growers are required to pay full attention to various aspects, such as weather, season, tree features, term of cultivation, soil and pot size, and decide the frequency of watering and amounts of water to give. Watering is intended not only to replenish moisture but to send fresh air into soil.

Water drainage. It refers to drainage of water from the bottom of a pot. It is also called ”mizuhake.” Not only water but oxygen must be supplied to tree roots to help them grow. After moisture between soil particles dries up, fresh air comes in and helps activate hairy roots smoothly. So, growers need to select proper potting composts that drain water smoothly and also should carefully study the placement, number and size of holes in the bottom of a pot.

Literally, termination of water supply. It refers to shortfall of water in a pot. ”Mizugire” causes leaves to wither or fall and branches to die. And finally, the tree itself will die. To cope with the phenomenon, irrigation is effective to restore the tree’s health at an early stage of ”mizugire.” But if symptoms from the phenomenon get worse, growers need to put the tree in the shade, give water, and continue moistening its leaves with water, and try to restore the tree’s health.

Bonsai tree grown from seed. It refers to planting seeds and cultivating them. This way of cultivation does not require great care and is suitable for beginners. The method is advantageous in that a tree can be grown as a bonsai plant from the start and that its ”nebari” surface roots develop sufficiently. However, it takes a great deal of time to grow a tree into a finished one, and the method may cause a transubstantiation phenomenon that makes a tree species unstable, disadvantageous points for the ”misho” cultivation method. The method is applicable for most tree species. Among ”shohaku” evergreen pines, it is often used for ”goyomatsu” (Japanese White Pine) and ”kuromatsu” (Japanese Black Pine) trees. ”Momiji” (Japanese Maple), ”keyaki” (Japanese Zelkova), ”kaede” (Maple) and ”soro” (Japanese Zelkova) are among ”zoki” deciduous trees to which the ”misho” cultivation method is applied.

Literally, trunk patterns. It refers to the curve line of a trunk that forms the basis of a tree form. Except for an upright trunk, most trunks draw curve lines in varying degrees. There are two types of ”mikimoyo” curve lines. One is a natural curve and the other an artificial one. An ideal curve line is one that is wide in the trunk root and tapers off toward the top. Tree of ”shakan” slant style and ”bunjingi” literal style draw typically gentle ”mikimoyo” curve lines. Trees of the ”kyokukan” curved style and ”takozukuri” octopus style are among those which draw strong curve lines.

Literally, trunk surface. It refers to the surface or bark of a trunk. This part graphically represents such elements as ancientry and antiquity that are important for bonsai appreciation. Whether the ”mikihada” trunk surface is old or young will determine the quality of the bonsai tree.

Literally, a formal pot. It refers to a container that is used to plant a bonsai tree for appreciation. In general, ”hombachi” pots lack aerial property and are not suitable for plant cultivation, so it is better to use a ”baiyobachi” (pot for cultivation) that is made of loose paste to grow and manage bonsai trees on a daily basis. As ”hombachi” pots are used for appreciation of bonsai plants, growers need to pay attention to the combination and matching with a bonsai tree in purchasing such a formal pot.
Literally, bones. The term refers to core elements of a tree, such as root parts, trunks and thick branches, which cannot be remade easily. ”Hone” can decide the individuality of a tree.

Literal style. One of the bonsai styles, ”bunjingi” refers to a tree of slim trunk with meaningful curves, of fewer branches and leaves, and of no useless elements. But such a tree is full of delicate emotion that brews poetic and artistic sentiment. Originally, a tree of this style was loved mainly by ”bunjin” (writers). So, it is called ”bunjingi,” literally meaning writers’ tree. ”Bunjingi” trees are highly popular but the number of trees of this style is very small because they must be grown while keeping their trunks slim for a long period of time. ”Akamatsu” (Japanese Red Pine) and ”goyomatsu” (Japanese White Pine) are typical species of tree of this style.

Literally, cutting old leaves. It refers to the work of cutting off old leaves from summer to autumn to provide sufficient sunlight and improve ventilation to the root parts of branches. Evergreen trees keep leaves for one year to one year and a half. Leaves that came out a year earlier or two years earlier are collectively called ”furuha” (old leaves). Cutting old leaves with scissors is particularly effective for ”goyomatsu” (Japanese White Pine) trees.

”Furi” refers to the curve line of a trunk that is the basis of a tree form. Some tools, such as wires, are used to build up the ”furi” curve line. Soft ”furi” curve lines are desirable for trunks. In general, ideal curve lines should be large in the lower trunks and small in the upper ones.

Literally, the bosom. It refers to root parts of tree branches that are close to tree trunks. The value goes up for a bonsai tree whose ”futokoro” is branchy. But, as those parts are usually unsunny and poorly ventilated, branches and buds are slow to grow there. If ”futeiga” indefinite buds come out from those parts, growers need to do pruning or wiring work, secure sufficient sunlight, and carefully nurture them.

Indefinite buds. The term refers to buds that come out from unexpected parts of plant, other than the stem, tips of branches and leaf axils from where buds usually come out. ”Futeiga” buds often come out from young trees or trees whose growth momentum is strong. ”Futeiga” buds come out from every part. Indefinite buds from under the surface at the root of a tree are called ”hikobae” and are to be taken off.

”Hibai” refers to the artificial replenishment of nutrition, such as fertilizer, in the course of cultivation. There are many nutritive substances in natural soil that are essential for plants to grow. However, those substances are not necessarily in a good chemical form for plants to absorb from roots, so there is a need to provide artificial fertilizers. Among such fertilizers are solid ones which dissolve in irrigation water and soak though soil. Liquid ones are mostly concentrates, so they should be attenuated before spraying. Besides the solid and liquid ones, there are soil-activating agents which transform chemical forms of natural nutritive substances in soil to help plants absorb them more easily.

”Hikobae” means the coming out of a ”futeiga” indefinite bud from under the surface at the root of a tree. It also refers to the indefinite bud itself. The phenomenon often occurs to frutescent, multi-trunk species of tree. If the situation is left untouched, the tree will likely weaken. It is best to remove such buds. In some species, such as ”zakuro” (pomegranate), the buds can be used to multiply by division.

Rock-like roots. The term refers to superior roots on the topsoil after two or more roots are knit together. The roots are called ”bankon.” Such roots are seen in many ”zoki” deciduous trees, such as ”buna” (Siebold’s Beech), ”momiji” (Japanese Maple) and ”himeshara” (Tall Stewartia), whose attraction is ”nebari” surface roots.

Semi-cascade. One of the bonsai styles and also one of the ”kengai” cascade styles. The trunk of a tree shows nutation and the tips of the trunk or branches fall above the base of the pot in the ”hankengi” semi-cascade style. Among many bonsai styles, the ”hankengi” semi-cascade style can work to instill deep naturalness and graciousness.

Wiring. It refers to the work of wiring trunks and branches of a bonsai tree to help shape it. Wiring is said to be most time-consuming and difficult in bonsai-related work but is one of the most important processes in bonsai cultivation. Wiring can shape a bonsai tree faster than ”hasami-zukuri” scissors work. Use of wires can cause a tree to discharge a plant hormone that promotes putting forth buds. Copper or aluminum wires are used. Wire is used from the bottom up to trunks and branches that need to be shaped. If wiring is too tight, it will bite into the trunk too fast, but if too loose, the trunk will not transform easily, so such work is difficult, often taking no less than one year. Lengthy wiring work, amounting to years, can help a bonsai tree develop true magnificence.

Burning of leaves. It refers to leaf tips running dry or leaves turning brownish or yellow and occurs because water absorbed from the root will not go to the leaves. The phenomenon often occurs from summer to early autumn. Leaves hit by the phenomenon will never be revived. The termination of water provision is the direct cause of the phenomenon. When a tree suffers from a disruption of balance in its water-absorbing and moisture-transpiration abilities, its leaves face trouble in the tissues to bring about such a phenomenon. A sufficient amount of water must therefore be provided to prevent the phenomenon. In addition, the use of a ”kanreisha” vinyl cover or ”yoshizu” bamboo blinds is effective in curbing extraordinary moisture transpiration, protecting plants from strong sunlight and preventing ”hayake” disaster in summer. Special attention should be paid to ”buna” (Siebold’s Beech), ”momiji” (Japanese Maple), ”himeshara” (Tall Stewartia) and ”soro” (Red-leaved hornbeam) trees, all of which are prone to ”hayake.”
Leaf bud. It refers to a bud that grows into a leaf.

Moistening leaves with water. ”Hamizu” differs from ”nemizu” (watering a tree at its root). The work is done to replenish water for leaves that dried up or to adjust leaves’ surface temperature. Giving water to leaves for a certain period of time is effective in preventing moisture transpiration from leaves, particularly after a tree was transplanted to a pot and lost much of its root, and also during the hot summer season. A ”joro” sprinkling can or a sprayer is used in the work.

The term refers to one or two trunks in a multi-trunk tree sprouting out to the right or left. Usually, a small trunk or trunks in a group planting are sprouting out. A bonsai tree with ”hanedashi” trunks is considered dynamic, so ”hanedashi” is an important factor in determining the value of a bonsai tree as a whole.

Thinning out leaves. It refers to the work of cutting old leaves to fix up a bonsai tree. The work reduces the number of leaves to curb the momentum of excessively strong leaf growth and to improve sunlight to and ventilation through exuberant leaves. Leaf thinning is to be done mainly for ”kuromatsu” (Japanese Black Pine) and ”akamatsu” (Japanese Red Pine) trees. It is usually supplementary work to back up ”mekiri” bud trimming to be done during a dormant period. Coupled with ”midoritsumi” (fresh-bud trimming), ”mekiri” (bud trimming) and ”mekaki” (second-bud trimming), the ”hanuki” work is important to shape branches and adjust a bonsai tree.

Floral bud. It refers to a bud that sends out a flower-blooming branch. There are a variety of floral buds, depending on tree species. In one case, a ”haname” floral stem appears at the end of a ”tocho-shi” branch, one that has become too long. On the other hand, such a bud will appear on a relatively short but thick branch. It is important to deepen knowledge about trees’ characteristics on forming floral buds, particularly for people to cultivate fruits and flowers in bonsai containers.

Refers to the volume and size to the right and left of a bonsai tree. Such an expression is often used to say the tree’s ”habari” measures certain centimeters from the end of the right branch to that of the left branch. In some cases, ”habari” refers to a tree’s outline. A combination of trunks, foliage and a pot will tell the ideal ”habari” of a bonsai tree.

The term refers to a bonsai tree that is transplanted into a pot after being grown in the field. Such trees grow in a short period of time and are traded at relatively low prices despite their large size. They are easily obtainable and popular. But it cannot be denied that such trees look less gorgeous than products grown in containers for a long time. What is important is to completely wipe off field soil from the tree before putting it into a pot.

An expression of good conditions of a bonsai tree. Literally, it means impulsion or momentum. In Japanese, it is ”hazumi” as a noun and ”hazumu” as a verb. The term is used when a bonsai tree and its trunks and branches are in good shape. Among examples of such a description is, ”Hazumi is seen in the branches,” meaning the tree branches are well-balanced, varied and dynamic. ”Hazumi is seen in the tree” is another expression.

Leaf features. It refers to characteristics of leaves, such as colors, forms, ways of their coming out and strength of their growth. A difference in leaf features could lead to a difference in the value even though the trees are of the same species. Generally, good leaf features for needle-leaved trees are said to be short, straight, bright and thick. In the case of ”zoki” deciduous trees, good leaf features are said to be small, shiny, bright and beautiful in the foliage season. The value of a bonsai tree goes up if it satisfies those conditions. As it is difficult to improve ”hasho” leaf features, full evaluation of them in advance is key to the purchase of a bonsai tree.

Literally, a running root. It refers to a root that grows much longer in soil than other roots. It is also called ”abare-ne” (ramp root). When a bonsai tree is drawn out of a pot, a long, thick and distinguished root is found among its fine roots. Then, it is ”hashiri-ne.” It is better to trim down or take away such a root at the time of transplantation because branches and leaves of a bonsai tree grow in a balanced manner only under even roots.

Literally, a running branch. It refers to a tree branch that grows much stronger than other branches. The phenomenon is often seen in ”zoki” deciduous trees. A powerful branch comes out when a tree goes off balance and extends its thick root into soil. If the situation is left as is, the branch’s root could grow too thick and fine branches may die, so early pruning work is required. If a certain ”hashiri-eda” branch cannot be removed in order to maintain the figure of a tree, wires should be used to adjust the tree form while paying attention to the tree’s whole balance.

Literally, scissors work. It refers to the work of pruning only with scissors to tune fine branches and to build up the tree form without relying on the tree-wiring technique. Usually, artists use wires to constrict tree buds that are trying to go up, in order to shape the tree form. The method is called ”meosae” (bud constricting). Some artists intentionally avoid ”meosae” in order to bring about a more natural look, and shape the trees only by pruning with scissors. The scissors work is said to bring about the quality of tree branches in accordance with the age of the tree.
A bonsai dressing-up style that uses a box-type display shelf. This style is used mainly to dress up ”shohin” small bonsai pieces.

Cutting leaves partially. It refers to the work of clipping parts of leaves when their size is random or they grow too large and lose beauty. The work is also done to prevent moisture transpiration from leaves in the grafting of ”zoki” deciduous trees.

Cutting leaves. It refers to the process of cutting leaves off with scissors or other cutting tools, except for leaf stalks. Usually, the work is done from mid-May to mid-June after fresh buds come out and firm up in spring. There are two different styles for the leaf-cutting work. One is to take away the whole leaves, and the other is to partially remove leaves whose growth is too vigorous. The work will be mainly done to remove leaves that grow too large, refresh them, and reduce their size. Small branches will sometimes come out after leaf stalks fall off. So, the leaf-cutting work is also aimed at adjusting plants’ growth momentum mainly for leaf bonsai and for some specific species that will help bonsai lovers enjoy the delicacy of fine branches in the winter. Leaf cutting will also adjust the timing of leaves coming out and pave the way for enthusiasts to enjoy more beautiful autumn leaves. As leaves that come out after the leaf-cutting work are usually thin and weak, they are susceptible to diseases, such as powdery mildew. So, anti-disease measures should be taken at an early stage.
Watering a bonsai tree at its root, but not at its crown. The term is used in contrast to ”hamizu” (moistening leaves with water).

Literally, a sleeping bud. It means a bud that comes out in fall or later will not burst into leaf next spring. Such a phenomenon will hit a tree that cannot obtain sufficient sunlight or ventilation, or an aged one that lacks vigor. In some cases, a bud could come out a year later. The ”nemurime” phenomenon often strikes ”shohaku” evergreen pine trees.
